prompt:
I need the front end for Aisle Lab. A teaching analytics workspace licensed by a university business school for its undergraduate retail management course, where students explore a realistic but fictional retailer's sales data to answer assignment questions.

Who's using it: Priya Natarajan, a third-year marketing major taking Retail Analytics (MKTG 341) this fall. She's comfortable with spreadsheets and pivot tables but has never worked with transaction-level data before. She's working on her laptop in the business school library the night before a deliverable is due.

What they're doing right now: Problem Set 4 asks whether the fictional chain's September 'Back to Lunchbox' promotion actually grew sales, or whether it just pulled purchases forward and took sales from neighboring products. She has already found that promoted snack SKUs sold 38% more units during the promo weeks. Now she needs to check three things: whether total category revenue rose, whether non-promoted juice boxes and granola bars fell over the same weeks, and whether sales dipped in the two weeks after the promo ended. She also has to see whether the effect looks different at the two suburban stores than at the four urban ones. Her answer must be a written claim backed by two or three exported figures, and the instructor has asked students to note any store or week that doesn't fit their story.

What's in the system at this point: Fenwick Market, a fictional six-store grocery chain: 18 months of point-of-sale records (Jan 2025 – Jun 2026), about 142,000 transactions and 611,000 line items across 1,214 SKUs in 14 categories. Each line item has date, store, SKU, category, unit price, discount applied and basket ID. A promotion log lists 27 promotions with start and end dates, discount depth and participating SKUs; 'Back to Lunchbox' ran Sep 1–21, 2025, at 20% off 46 SKUs. Store attributes include square footage, urban/suburban, and the opening date of the Halvorsen Ave store, which opened mid-period in March 2025. Also loaded: the course's assignment prompt, a grading rubric with 4 criteria, and Priya's saved explorations from earlier problem sets.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
